title: "Zero-shot Classification"
description: "Classifying inputs into candidate labels without task-specific labeled examples for those labels."
term: "Zero-shot Classification"
letter: "Z"
category: "Machine Learning"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

Zero-shot classification asks a model to assign an input to one of several
labels even though it was not trained on labeled examples for that particular
classification task.

## Technical explanation

In language-model approaches, candidate labels may be rendered as text and
scored against the input or supplied in a prompt. In embedding-based
approaches, the input and label descriptions are encoded and compared.
Performance depends on the pretrained model, candidate wording, label set,
calibration, and domain match; “zero-shot” does not mean the model learned
nothing relevant during pretraining.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Zero-shot classification can bootstrap prototypes, triage new categories, or
handle changing taxonomies without collecting task-specific training data.
It should be evaluated on representative labeled examples before being used
for high-impact decisions.

## How it works

Define mutually understandable candidate labels, encode or prompt the input
with those labels, and select or score candidate outputs. For open-ended
deployment, define abstention behavior and measure sensitivity to label
phrasing and class imbalance.

## Practical example

Classify incoming support requests as billing, account access, or technical
issues using a pretrained natural-language inference model. Compare results
against a labeled evaluation set and route low-confidence cases to review.

## Common misconceptions

- Zero-shot does not guarantee accurate performance on unseen domains or
  labels.
- Changing candidate labels can change predictions even when the input stays
  the same.
